location: Rio de Janeiro, Brazil — Candelária Church
address: Igreja de Nossa Senhora da Candelária, Praça Pio X, Centro, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil
recipient: Mrs. John Woy[?], 4 Stouffer Z3[?], Lawrence, Kansas, U.S.A. (later forwarded c/o USIS Office, Consulado Americano, Porto Alegre, RG do Sul, Brasil — added in red ink)
notes: Front caption: “Rio de Janeiro / GB / Brasil — Igreja da Candelária / Candelaria Church,” photo by Fulvio Roiter, published by Gráfica Franco Brasileira Ltda. “GB” refers to the Estado da Guanabara, the short-lived Brazilian state (1960–1975) that Rio de Janeiro formed after Brasília became the national capital — this card dates from squarely within that period, less than a year before the April 1964 military coup. Candelária Church itself was built 1775–1898 on the site of a 1609 chapel, raised in thanks by a shipwrecked sea captain and his wife who survived a storm in Guanabara Bay; it was, for a time, the largest and wealthiest church in imperial Brazil. Brazilian airmail (“Correio Aéreo”) postage with Duque de Caxias and José Bonifácio definitive stamps. Message: “Dear Penney – July 31. It just dawned on me, I don't know your new address – I trust this will be forwarded. We spent the 1st 3 weeks near Rio (1st week in a small resort town near Rio) in a constant flurry of classes (Portuguese & history), museums, sight-seeing, cocktail parties, swimming, etc. There are 9 or 10 Fulbrighters here – a good group (by that I mean I like them). July 29 I flew to Porto Alegre – an interesting town & from what I've seen so far, the people are very warm & friendly. I wrote a long letter to Mother – Impressions of P.A. – I asked her to read it to you or give you a copy. more later – write! Love, Mary” Mary appears to be a U.S. Fulbright exchange student in Brazil in 1963, and the card was later re-routed through the American consulate to follow her onward to Porto Alegre.

address: 5646 Milton St. (North Central Expressway), Dallas, TX
recipient: Mr. & Mrs. Felix Yoder, Berne, Ind.
notes: Front caption: “Meadows Building, Dallas, Texas. Located on the North Central Expressway, the Meadows Building is unique in that it has the largest ‘hanging roof garden’ outside Rockefeller Center. The building covers six acres, has parking for 500 cars. Built by the employees of the General American Oil Co. of Texas as a trust for employee pensions. Color by John Messina.” Published by Texas Post Card Co., Dallas / made by Dexter, West Nyack, N.Y. Completed in 1955, the Meadows Building was the first Dallas office tower built outside downtown, designed by architect J.N. MacCammon and named for company president Algur H. Meadows; it was employee-owned through a 1950 pension trust, and its famous hanging garden (by Lambert Landscaping) was removed in 1984 and later restored in a 2020s renovation. 4-cent Lincoln stamp, postmarked Dallas, Tex., 7:30 PM, 30 Nov 1963 — just eight days after President Kennedy's assassination in Dallas on November 22, 1963. Message: “11-30-63. Dear Folks: We got here about 9:00 Thursday morn. OK but tired. It started to rain just before we got to Texas and rained gently the rest of the way. We are seeing the place that saddened the nation. The girls are trying hard to make our stay pleasant. Sam's went on south this morning. Expecting to start for home next Wed morning. Love Dad & Mother” — “the place that saddened the nation” almost certainly refers to Dealey Plaza and the assassination site, making this an ordinary family road-trip card caught up in the immediate aftermath of a defining national tragedy.
feed_description: A Dallas postcard mailed just eight days after JFK's assassination — ‘we are seeing the place that saddened the nation,’ a family writes home from the Meadows Building.
